name: weather_shadow_visibility
_comment: §13a: a cloudy-day shadow has to be visible, not merely computed.
moon_shadow_render reads MatBases.SunShadow.color.r — the FINAL composed shadow colour the
shader draws with, Color.Lerp(white, colors.shadow, alpha). Its name is from §6a but the value
is the general one, and it is the only measurement that distinguishes 'the alpha is right' from
'you can see a shadow' — which is exactly the distinction this fix is about.
Noon at latitude 20 so the sun is high and ShadowIntensityFromElevation has saturated; the alpha
is then governed by weather alone. Expected values computed offline from WeatherDimmingMath.
The A/B toggle is weather_dimming, because §13a is gated on it: with §13 off, vanilla's flat
0.92 is the only weather softening there is and the patch deliberately stands down.
EVERY expected value here tracks TWO shipped-preset knobs, so recompute all of them when either
moves: Presets.Cinematic.WeatherDimming (0.20) sets the alpha's weather term, and
Presets.Cinematic.ShadowStrength (0.8) multiplies the finished alpha in Patch_ShadowStrength.

steps._comment: Clear noon is the reference and must be untouched: the patch substitutes Clear's OWN colour, so on Clear it is a no-op by construction. The colour is vanilla's skyColorsDay.shadow of 0.718; the reading is above it because the alpha is not 1 — 0.994 of a full-strength shadow times the preset's 0.8 slider renders 0.7757, a 22.4% darkening.
Rain at noon with §13 OFF — the patch stands down, so this captures the shipped artifact: vanilla's flat 0.92 colour, a 6.4% darkening that no correct alpha can reach past.

Rain at noon with §13 ON — the fix. Cloud opacity is 1.0 (every non-Clear vanilla weather shares one skyColorsDay), so alpha is ShadowContrastFactor(1.0, MaxDimming) and the colour is now Clear's 0.718. On the shipped Cinematic preset that is 0.4333, times the near-1 elevation term and the 0.8 shadow-strength slider -> alpha 0.3446, rendered 0.9028: a 9.7% darkening against the 2.8% it used to be.

Fog and a hard blizzard read identically to Rain — same skyColorsDay, so same opacity. Probed to PIN that, not to celebrate it: §13a does not make weathers differ from each other, and a future change that thinks it did should fail here.

LOW SUN — the block that produces a legible picture, added after the noon frames turned out to show nothing. Shadow LENGTH is cot(elevation), so noon's 81.7-degree sun casts 0.15 cells: the contrast fix was working and there was no shadow there to look at. Hour 5.0 puts the sun at 13.4 degrees and the shadow at 4.20 cells — 28x longer — while contrast barely moves (8.9% against noon's 9.7%), because ShadowIntensityFromElevation has saturated and PenumbraContrastFactor is still 0.91. Everything below is a screenshot pair first and a probe second.

Night must be untouched: §6a's Patch_MoonShadowColor owns colors.shadow below the horizon and §13a stands down there, so this reads §6a's own value and not Clear's 0.718. At day 40 hour 2 the tick-derived cycle is 0.6722 — a 73.5%-lit WANING GIBBOUS, not a full moon. Assuming a full moon here is exactly the mistake this comment exists to prevent.
steps._comment2: §6b RE-BASELINE: 0.8531 -> 0.8023. The old model was linear in illuminated fraction, so a 73.5%-lit moon cast 73.5% of full strength (0.2057 alpha). §6b makes strength a contrast RATIO instead, and the sun is 47 degrees down here — the sky is at the 0.001 lux starlight floor, so this moon's 0.087 lux dominates it 87:1 and the shadow is at 0.2768, near the cap. Recompute: MoonLux(0.735, 73.2) = 0.267 * 0.735^3.5 * sin(73.2) = 0.0870; contrast = 0.0870/(0.0870+0.001) = 0.9886; strength = 0.9886 * 0.28 = 0.2768; times the preset's 0.8 slider = an alpha of 0.2215, which against §6a's 0.1071 shadow colour renders 1 - 0.2215*(1-0.1071) = 0.8023.
steps._comment3: Phase still matters under §6b, but at the twilight end (WHEN a shadow appears) rather than as a proportional dimming in full darkness — see moon_shadow_twilight_fade.json. In a sky this dark, gibbous and full are within 0.003 of each other.
